messages.body_plain:
I am a new user attempting to estimate densities of a seabird from line transect surveys done at-sea.  For our MCDS model examining the effects of beaufort sea state (as a categorical variable, with 3 levels due to me merging some uncommon sea states) I’m getting errors of “mismatched strata”, like this:

**Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata- 2   1**

**Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata- 3   2**

**Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata- 4   3**
In the distance help, I noticed that for these errors it says to contact the program authors and so I’m asking for help from the listerv and hoping someone can point me to my error.  I attached the log file, plus a screenshot of the project browser data tab.

Other than these errors, the results of this MCDS analysis look more-or-less fine. The results tab produces aic values, and the density estimates and CIs are reasonable and compare well to our CDS model without beaufort.

I input the data using year as our ‘region’, interval as our ‘line transect’ and then the observations represent observations of our birds from individual line transects (total of 85), and blank lines (but which contain beaufort) are transects that we surveyed but did not detect birds.  I am attempting to estimate density with mcds for each year and ideally with a separate year/stratum level detection function.  The problem occurs when I request stratum level detection function in the estimate tab.  When I request the global detection function in mcds, the analysis runs ok (though with warnings).

 Thank you,
Teresa

Teresa

I've had a closer look at the screen grab you sent, as well as your project description.

In the lingo of Distance, region is equivalent of stratum--so that makes sense to use this as a place to put "year".  But you've lost me when you describe "interval as our line transect".  That's not going to work.  Transects need to be transects--respecting the design used to collect the data.  I would structure your data differently; and in doing so, perhaps resolve your "mismatched strata" mystery.

Do you wish to produce just a single estimate per year; hence pooling across your repeated visits per year?  That's the sense I get.  You have many choices for organising the data, one scheme might be one in which the transect label (which is alphanumeric) could be 1a for first visit to line 1, 1b for second visit, etc.  If you wish to produce visit-specific estimates (assuming sufficient detections) and the same transects across visits,  you could consider a data structure such as that used in the Montrave line transect analysis where visit is recorded as a covariate in the Observation layer.  See our supplement to the Distance sampling-methods and applications book at http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/DS.M&A/  (look for the Distance project under Distance GUI analysis/Distance projects)

At the observation level, record only data associated with detections (perp.dist, group size and Beaufort). Records in the observation layer with no distances is weird.

See where this takes you in the analysis of your multi-year project.

I've run into a bit of a problem getting sample level density estimates from my point-count data and was wondering if anyone had any suggestions. Thanks for any and all help, I really appreciate it.

messages.body_plain:
Hi John, hi listfolk,

To my knowledge, there is no "cutoff" for concurvity that can be
generally applied, mainly because this is still a somewhat experimental
technique in the very early stages of development. For the same reason,
I don't have too much guidance to offer on which of the measures would
be most appropriate. My usual approach is to look at the results for the
three metrics (probably paying more attention to the "estimate" type),
look at the measures then check to see if those terms with higher values
change model results when they are removed. Assessing that kind of model
structure instability seems like the most useful application of concurvity.

As for the asymmetry of the resulting matrix, I think this is okay since
the measure displayed is related to the values of the norm of one smooth
divided by the norm of another (max of the norms or whatever). symmetric
entries are reciprocals of each other (e.g., f/g or g/f) but I don't
think there's any reason to think that these should be identical. That
being said, they probably should be about the same order I would think.

The ?concurvity manual page also has some more (albeit technical) detail.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Jochen

This is a topic that has come up several times on the list; not specifically in the context of the mrds package, but about aerial surveys in general.  The issue is less about the effective strip with than about the fitting of the detection function and subsequent estimation of density or abundance.

You ask which of the two approaches to employ.  Here is a reply from Len Thomas dated 14June2004

Having left truncated, you have two options: (1) fit a detection function to the truncated data as is.  This does not assume that g(x)=1 at the truncation point. (2) subtract the truncation distance from all data -- effectively move the centreline out to be at the truncation distance.  This then assumes that g(x)=1 at the truncation distance.  The former strategy has a weaker assumption, but will give higher variance as the detection function close to the line has no data to tell it where to fit -- it will be relying on the data from > the left truncation point and the assumed shape of the detection function.
For a non-aerial survey perceptive, have a look at Buckland et al. (2001) section 8.4.3.  There you will find a discussion of terrestrial nest data for pintail ducks, where the data were analysed in the two ways you describe, resulting in these two figures:

Have a look at the remainder of that section of the text for further details.

Andrea

I'm mildly confused about how this post from 2006 came to be part of this message; but I'll take things at face value and assume you want to calculate effect size and are wondering whether the Z-statistic shown in eqn 3.102 of Buckland et al. (2001:85) is appropriate.  The answer is that this calculation is appropriate, unless degrees of freedom (shown in eqn 3.101) is small, i.e. <30.  This degrees of freedom calculation is a combination of uncertainties in the two density estimates.

The apt analogy is not cluster size, but rather  a cue-counting survey; with trees being the equivalent of cues.  You know multiple trees are used by an individual; hence you want to multiply  your tree density estimate by 1/(trees per individual) to estimate individuals per area.  This is equivalent to the adjustment of cue density into animal density with the conversion factor of cue rate.

Another analogy would be dung surveys; you measure density of something created by the animal, rather than the animal itself.  Dung surveys are more complicated that what you are doing because of the need to estimate creation and disappearance rates.

Essentially you can use the delta method approximation, based upon "squared CVs add".  Assume "TD" is your estimate of tree density and "UT" is your estimate of used trees (per individual), and you wish to estimate precision of animal density "A":

​

If you want se(A), you can obtain this by

se(A) = cv(A) * A

For more details, look into the distance sampling literature under the term "indirect surveys"; e.g. Section 9.3 & 9.4 of Buckland et al. (2015).

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Deciding on bin numbers and truncation
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Deciding on bin numbers and truncation
messages.body_plain:
Brigham

A couple of comments: warning are not the same as errors.  The warning is suggesting there is a "spike" in your data at distance > 0.  That's not inherently wrong; you need simply to understand why that hump in your data exists.

Using a small CV is a *bad* idea for model selection; it may lead to confidence intervals that are too narrow to include the true parameter.

General rule: use exact distances if possible, they provide more information about the fit of your model to your data.  Bin if there is rounding to preferred distances (better yet, don't round to preferred distances when collecting data).

When noting differences in density estimates from different analyses, place those differences in the context of the precision of the estimates themselves.  A 5% difference between analyses is small if the CVs are 30%.

All of my models have a detection probability >1 despite different truncation and binning techniques.  If I am understanding everything correctly, I never added any adjustment terms into my models.  My current best model is a half-normal cosine with right and left truncation.

Logically, it doesn't make sense to me that detection probability could be >1 so I'm trying to understand this.  I appreciate any insight you might have for me!

On Tuesday, November 18, 2014 at 3:00:47 AM UTC-6, Stephen Buckland wrote:

>Thanks, Steve.  Yes, removing the cosine adjustment (/Adjust=CO) keeps things below 1.0.  I'll probably fit the series of data sets I have >with the cosine adjustment and without the cosine adjustment and pick the smallest AICc except when any of the estimates exceed >1.0.  Does that sound too convoluted?

That should be OK.  Personally, I’m not a fan of using adjustment terms in mcds.  They are there to put ‘wiggles’ in the detection function, if one of the key functions cannot fit the data well on its own, so giving greater flexibility.  Modelling covariates in the detection function also gives greater flexibility, and it’s not often that you get a big improvement in fit by including adjustments in addition to covariates, unless there are problems with the data (e.g. substantial rounding, responsive movement, etc).

>I'm assuming that while the estimation procedure does force the probability to be 1.0 a zero distance, the likelihood (and therefore the >AICc) is based on a general curve fitting procedure rather than restricting the maximum estimate to be no greater than 1.0 (especially >when using the cosine adjustment).

If you have no adjustment, this cannot occur, because the models for the detection function are non-increasing.  However, once you include adjustments, there is no guarantee that the fitted probability density function is non-increasing.  Because we obtain the fitted detection function by scaling the density function so that it is one at zero distance, that detection function might then increase above one.  The cds engine of Distance deals with this by incorporating a penalty term in the likelihood, that results in the fitted function being (almost) non-increasing.  The mcds engine does not have this feature.

Steve

Teresa

I've spent some time looking at your Distance project and I want to let you know what I've found.  Unfortunately, I have seen an anomaly, but I don't know its complete resolution.  My suspicion is that few Distance users have analysed datasets with >10 strata, and even fewer of those users have incorporated covariates into their detection function models.  I'm afraid this email is a bit lengthy as the search for clues unfolds.

The analysis that throws the "mismatched strata" error is the analysis that does the following:

- produces year(stratum)-specific detection functions
- this detection function includes a covariate (sea state)
- model selection operates so as to choose on a stratum-by-stratum basis which key function (hn or haz) to select)

>From what I can deduce, all goes swimmingly for the first 10 (strata)years (2001-2010) of the analysis.  However, in 2011, there is an anomaly.  In all other years, there are detections recorded in sea states 0, 1, and 2.  However in 2011, there are detections made only in sea states 1 and 2 (no detections in sea state 1).  Might the inconsistent number of covariate levels in this stratum cause some difficulties?  Consequently, there is one fewer parameter in this hazard rate model, than in hazard rate models for other years.  Contrast these two parameter estimate tables, first 2009:

 Model
    Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(34))

     s = A(33) * Exp(fcn(A(35)) + fcn(A(36)))
    Parameter A(33) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
    Parameter A(34) is the power parameter.
    Parameter A(35) is the coefficient of level 0 of factor covariate BEAUFORT.
    Parameter A(36) is the coefficient of level 1 of factor covariate BEAUFORT.

Then 2011:

 Model
    Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(42))

     s = A(41)Exp(fcn(A(43)))
    Parameter A(41) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
    Parameter A(42) is the power parameter.
    Parameter A(43) is the coefficient of level 1 of factor covariate BEAUFORT.
The mystery then deepens when the covariate-level-specific detection function histograms are shown for the 2 sea states in 2011:

Look closely at the plot titles to notice I didn't mistakenly past the same plot into this email twice.

More mysteries continue when looking further into the results for this particular model.

The bookmark tab labelled "Density estimate/11. 2011" later in the printout ought to give a recapitulation of the previous parameter estimation, along with estimates of D and N.  Have a look:

 Stratum       : 11. 2011
 Effort        :    1828.000

 # observations:   951

 Model
    Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*s**2))

     s = A(37) * Exp(fcn(A(38)) + fcn(A(39)))
    Parameter A(37) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
    Parameter A(38) is the coefficient of level 0 of factor covariate BEAUFORT.
    Parameter A(39) is the coefficient of level 1 of factor covariate BEAUFORT.

              Point        Standard    Percent Coef.        95% Percent
  Parameter   Estimate       Error      of Variation     Confidence Interval
  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------
    f(0)     0.10195E-01  0.23184E-03       2.27      0.97498E-02  0.10660E-01
    p        0.56977      0.13210E-01       2.32      0.54443      0.59629
    ESW       102.56       2.3777           2.32       97.997       107.33
    n/L      0.52024      0.12945          24.88      0.30855      0.87717
    DS        2.2186      0.50464          22.75       1.3758       3.5778
    E(S)      2.0166      0.28926E-01       1.43       1.9607       2.0742
    D         4.4742       1.0197          22.79       2.7729       7.2194
    N         3012.0       686.45          22.79       1867.0       4860.0
  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------

 ---------------------------------
 Density: Numbers/Sq. kilometers
     ESW: meters

 Detection probability   :   1.0

Several curiosities arise:

- what had previously been a hazard rate model fitted to this stratum, has now become a half normal key function
- where previous print-out had shown 851 detections in the 2011 stratum, now there appears 951 (the same number of detections as the 2012 stratum)
- have a look at the percentage of variation in the density estimate attributable to  encounter rate variation.

To be honest,   I have doubted my sanity several times.

What remedies did I try?

- I tried, via the data filter, to omit 2011 from the analysis.  Unfortunately that merely caused many more problems.
- I repeated the analysis, keeping everything the same except removing the sea state covariate.  That removed the "mismatch" error and consistent summary tables in two places in the output.  If I needed to produce a report about this species, these are the results I would present.  The differences in the abundance point estimates between the model with and without the sea-state covariate is on the order of 5-10%, with the CV bouncing between 25 and 30%.  Precision is virtually unchanged between estimate using or not using the sea state covariate (because >90% of the uncertainty is driven by variation in encounter rate; hardly any uncertainty is associated with the parameter estimates of the detection function given the large samples you are working with).

We will have a look "under the hood" of Distance, but my suspicion rests with datasets that have >10 strata and are using covariates in the detection function (as both Teresa and Matt have indicated).  The solution at the moment seems to be eliminating the detection function covariate portion of the modelling.
